did_you_know.text: The heading presents the psalm as “A miktam of David” and adds the purpose “for teaching.” It also includes the musical or liturgical term “To Shushan Eduth.”

At the beginning of the psalm, the background of conflicts with Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah, and Edom is mentioned. According to the text, Joab struck down Edom in the Valley of Salt, and the number of dead given is twelve thousand.
The distress is described as a direct appeal to God: “You have rejected us; you have broken us.” At the very beginning of the psalm, a request for a change in the situation appears: “Restore us.”
The nation’s upheaval is described through the image of an earthquake and cracks in the land. Alongside this picture of devastation comes a request to heal and restore what has been damaged.
The poet describes the people’s painful experience through the image of “the wine of staggering”—a drink symbolizing suffering, turmoil, and affliction.

Alongside the description of distress, the psalm says that God gives those who fear him a “banner.” In the biblical context, a banner is also a raised flag or sign, so here it symbolizes gathering, protection, and hope.

The central request in the verse is that salvation should rescue God’s “beloved.” Thus, the people are described not merely as an army or a community in distress, but also as those connected to God by loyalty and affection.

After the prayer of distress comes a declaration that God has spoken in his holiness, and the speaker responds with joy. In the same sequence, Shechem and the Valley of Succoth are mentioned as part of a description of control over or division of the land.

The psalm lists regions and tribes of Israel: Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah. Ephraim is described as “the stronghold of my head,” while Judah has the role of a “lawgiver”—a symbol of leadership and legislation.

Moab, Edom, and Philistia appear as enemies on the political and military stage. Yet the conclusion emphasizes that human strength is not enough: “Human salvation is worthless,” whereas confidence lies in the fact that “with God we shall perform mighty deeds.”
